claim: In a randomized trial of 50 UK intelligence analysts, ACH did not improve probability accuracy; the no-method control was slightly better on raw error.
quote: ACH failed to improve intelligence analysts’ probabilistic judgments about alternative hypotheses
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Do not run an ACH matrix by default; test it against plain vote on split cases only.

claim: Raw mean absolute error was 0.26 for ACH vs 0.21 for control (p=.14, medium effect favoring control); after coherentization both were 0.15.
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Boundary: the null is small-N, so treat as no evidence of gain, not proof of harm.

claim: ACH group probabilities for four exclusive hypotheses summed to 1.77 vs 1.54 for control (ideal 1.0): ACH did not fix unpacking.
quote: Control 1.54 vs. ACH 1.77, both well above 1.0
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Always renormalize multi-hypothesis probabilities in code.

claim: Recalibration (coherentization) cut error 35% (0.23 to 0.15) and averaging all 50 analysts cut it 61% (to 0.09); post-processing beat the technique.
quote: recalibration and aggregation methods substantially improved accuracy
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Program step: normalize then average several varied-prompt samples; correlated samples will shrink the gain.

claim: ACH-trained analysts tracked true cue usefulness far better (r=.68 vs .17) yet this did not yield better final probabilities: a trained sub-skill did not transfer to the outcome.
quote: ACH correlation with probability gain was .68 vs. .17 for control
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Measure diagnosticity scoring separately from final accuracy; make the program consume it (for example pick the next test by it).

claim: In 227 participants over six cases with uncertain evidence, ACH gave no coherence advantage and was slightly less reliable across matched case pairs (.22 vs .18, p=.051).
quote: Participants who used ACH were less reliable across isomorphic cases than control participants
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: Log run-to-run consistency of any matrix step; a method can add variance.

claim: Only the ACH group showed pseudo-diagnosticity: non-diagnostic evidence still moved ratings toward the favored hypothesis at about 30% of the effect of fully diagnostic evidence.
quote: Non-diagnostic evidence still shifted ratings toward the hypothesis it favored, at about 30% of the impact of fully diagnostic evidence
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: Filter in code: drop evidence marked consistent with all hypotheses before counting.

claim: The authors conclude ACH may impair judgment, and both groups were too conservative against Bayesian benchmarks.
quote: ACH does not benefit judgment and, in fact, might impair judgment.
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: Treat structured doubt as a hypothesis to A/B, with a kill rule if consistency drops.

claim: In a 50-analyst randomized test, analysts trained in ACH did not complete all steps, evidence on confirmation bias was mixed, and ACH may raise inconsistency and error.
quote: ACH may increase judgment inconsistency and error.
title: The "analysis of competing hypotheses" in intelligence analysis
transfer: A program executes every step, removing the skipped-step failure; this is the main reason a human null may not carry to an agent.

claim: A RAND review found the US intelligence community pushes structured techniques but has made little effort to measure whether they improve analysis; a pilot found only wider outcome coverage, not accuracy.
title: Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community
transfer: Do not cite SAT popularity as evidence; require our own A/B. Direct fetch returned 403 this session, claim is from the earlier brief's search snippet.

claim: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a hidden-rule task, proposing tests that support their hypothesis; counterexample prompting raised rule discovery from 42% to 56%.
title: Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
transfer: Falsification prompt only where a test oracle gives feedback; boundary is exploration tasks.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback struggles and can lower accuracy: a failed-critique result relevant to devil's advocate steps.
quote: their performance even degrades after self-correction
authors: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Critique and red-team calls must be tied to an external check; otherwise discard or skip.

claim: Models fail mainly at locating errors, not fixing them: they struggle to find mistakes even in clear cases, but correct well when told where the error is.
quote: poor self-correction performance stems from LLMs' inability to find logical mistakes
title: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
transfer: A key-assumptions or red-team step is only as good as error localization; have code or a test point to the suspect step.

claim: LLMs struggle to identify fallacious reasoning steps, which limits the validity of self-verification.
quote: existing LLMs could struggle to identify fallacious reasoning steps accurately
title: A Closer Look at the Self-Verification Abilities of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
transfer: Do not let an LLM judge overturn an answer on its own say-so.

claim: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat simpler prompting such as self-consistency, and is sensitive to settings.
quote: do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies
title: Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
transfer: Baseline every adversarial step against same-cost majority vote.

claim: Multi-agent LLM system gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal; 14 failure modes in 1,600+ traces include inter-agent misalignment and weak task verification.
quote: their performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal
title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
transfer: Add a verification step that is checked by code, and log which failure mode kills runs.

claim: Five state-of-the-art assistants show sycophancy, and humans and preference models sometimes prefer sycophantic over correct answers, so a critic or judge can be pulled toward the stated answer.
quote: five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across four varied free-form text-generation tasks
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
transfer: Give critics the task without the leader's reasoning where possible, and avoid asking the model to agree.
